summary: Specifies the 0-RTT TCP Convert Protocol, an experimental way for a Transport Converter proxy to help deploy TCP extensions such as Multipath TCP. The service adds no extra delay because the conversion information is sent with the first data.

eli5.summary: A helper translates for you so you can speak a new language to a server that only knows the old one, without waiting.

questions: how can multipath tcp be deployed through a proxy
how can tcp extensions be deployed without server support
subtitle: A proxy translates extended TCP to standard TCP with no extra delay.

tldr.problem: TCP extensions like Multipath TCP take years to deploy because they require changes on both the client and server; servers often cannot be upgraded as quickly as clients.
tldr.mechanism: A Transport Converter proxy (a network function) sits between clients and servers, converting between a TCP extension on the upstream connection and standard TCP on the downstream connection, allowing clients to use extensions even when servers do not yet support them.
tldr.outcome: Extensions can be deployed and tested faster because support from servers is no longer a blocker. Clients can also learn whether a given server supports an extension natively and bypass the converter when the server is ready.

today: RFC 8803 is Experimental. It was published as a result of real deployment experience (5G bonding with 4G using MPTCP proxies) and is ready for wider implementation and testing. Transport Converters have been deployed in mobile networks to enable Multipath TCP connectivity.

sections.title: The Deployment Gap for TCP Extensions
sections.content:
Transport protocols evolve: TCP gets new options like Selective Acknowledgments, Window Scale, and (recently) Multipath TCP. Some improvements, like changing the initial congestion window, work with just a client upgrade. But options that require new TCP header fields or semantic changes need both client and server to support them. History shows this takes many years—a decade for some options. Wireless devices in particular want features like Multipath TCP's ability to bond WLAN and cellular links, but servers worldwide cannot be upgraded quickly enough.

This RFC specifies a Transport Converter: a network proxy deployed by the operator that a client connects to. The client uses the new TCP extension (like Multipath TCP) when talking to the Converter; the Converter translates that connection to standard TCP when reaching the server. This is called the 0-RTT TCP Convert Protocol because the conversion information is sent in the initial SYN packet—adding no extra round-trip time.
sections.eli5: A helper can translate between you and a server that does not speak your language yet, making the handshake instant instead of slow.

sections.title: How the Transport Converter Works
sections.content:
Three roles: Clients, Transport Converters, and Servers. The client is configured (statically or by policy) with the address of one or more Converters and which TCP extensions they support. When the client wants to use an extension, it connects to the Converter instead of directly to the server, placing the server's address and port in the initial SYN payload. The Converter immediately initiates a standard TCP connection to that server without waiting for a response from the client—this is the 0-RTT design. Only when the server accepts the connection does the Converter confirm it to the client.

The Converter maintains two connections: the upstream connection (client to Converter) and the downstream connection (Converter to server). User data is simply proxied between them. The Converter can operate in two modes: address preservation (the server sees the client's IP) or address sharing (the Converter uses a pool of addresses). With Multipath TCP, all subflows on the upstream may be proxied through a single TCP connection downstream.
sections.eli5: You tell the helper your destination and they immediately start a trip there, then connect you once they arrive. You do not have to wait for them to talk to the server first.

sections.title: The Convert Protocol Messages
sections.content:
Clients and Converters exchange Convert Protocol messages in the payload of SYN, SYN+ACK, or ACK packets. Messages are placed first in the bytestream, before any application data. The fixed header is 32 bits: an 8-bit version (currently 1), an 8-bit total message length, and a 16-bit magic number (0x2263) to distinguish Convert messages from application data.

After the header come Type-Length-Value (TLV) fields. The RFC defines several TLVs: an Info TLV listing what the client is trying to do, a Supported TCP Extensions TLV naming which extensions the Converter handles, a Connect TLV with the destination address and port, an Extended TCP Header TLV carrying negotiated options, a Cookie TLV for optional replay protection, and an Error TLV for reporting failures. By using TLVs, the protocol can be extended with new features without changing the core message structure.
sections.eli5: A structured conversation between the client and helper about what needs to happen, sent in the very first packet.

sections.title: Support for Specific TCP Extensions
sections.content:
The RFC discusses how the Converter handles various TCP options. Basic options like Window Scale and Selective Acknowledgments are straightforward. Multipath TCP is the primary use case: when a client uses Multipath TCP to the Converter, the Converter strips the MP_CAPABLE option and sends plain TCP to the server. If the server replies without MP_CAPABLE, the Converter tells the client the server does not support Multipath TCP, so the client knows it can connect directly in the future. If the server does support Multipath TCP, the Converter informs the client, and the client gains this knowledge for future connections.

TCP Fast Open is handled by allowing data in the SYN packet (like TFO does) but without consuming the TCP header space that a TFO Cookie would use; the Convert Protocol includes its own optional Cookie TLV in the payload. TCP-AO (Authentication Option) cannot be converted because the authentication covers the full TCP header and modifying it would break the signature.
sections.eli5: Different TCP options are handled in different ways: some pass through, some are translated, some cannot work through a converter at all.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that Transport Converters MUST be explicitly configured by the client or network operator—this is not a transparent proxy. End-to-end TLS encryption between client and server is supported and unaffected by the conversion; the Converter is only a TCP-level relay.

Security considerations include: Ingress filtering to prevent spoofing the Converter's IP, authentication and authorization so only allowed clients use the Converter, denial-of-service protection (the optional Cookie TLV can limit replay attacks), and prevention of traffic theft (only clients with proper authorization should be able to initiate connections). The Converter should log connections for accountability. The scope is explicitly single administrative domain: a network operator owns both the client environment and the Converter. Future third-party Converters would need additional mutual authentication.
sections.eli5: You have to explicitly ask to use the helper (not a secret middleman), and the helper can check that it is really you.
